claim: Data centers will destroy our community.
scope: The speaker’s own community where data centers are proposed, as the headline implies; here, DeKalb County, Georgia.
time_horizon: Future, if proposed data centers are built; no date given.
occurrence: Lightly generalized from Gina Mangham of the group Renew DeKalb, quoted by CBS News Atlanta (Nakell Williams, November 18, 2025) about proposals for data centers in DeKalb County, Georgia: “I believe this will destroy our community.” West Virginia Watch (Caity Coyne, May 28, 2025) quoted Tucker County resident Nikki Forrester saying of a proposed data center: “Honestly, I feel like if this happens, it will destroy this place.”

P1.reason: A prediction about one community; its certainty is scored under P3 and its severity under W1. No distinct problem with how current evidence is described.

P2.reason: Refers to one community facing specific proposals, not every town; no distinct scope problem beyond the severity scored under W1.

sources.locator: Paragraphs on the DeKalb zoning text amendment and data campus proposals

P3.reason: States a certain outcome. Proposals can be rejected or changed (the Prince William Digital Gateway rezoning was voided in court and a developer abandoned it; New York paused permits for new hyperscale projects), and local effects depend on siting, zoning and how utilities split costs.

sources.locator: Paragraphs on Compass ending its appeal and the project “may never see a single facility built”
Paragraphs on discretionary permits paused for up to a year

W1.reason: “Destroy” turns real but bounded costs into total ruin. Inspected evidence documents noise that affects well-being but does not damage hearing, few permanent jobs and pressure on regional power prices, alongside large tax revenue in some host counties; no inspected source shows a host community destroyed.

sources.locator: Paragraph on 38% of General Fund revenue and the tax rate

W2.reason: No human-like agency is attributed to AI; people decide where data centers are built.

evidence_limitations: Most detailed official evidence comes from Virginia, the largest US data-center market; other states and smaller sites may differ.
Future household bill increases are modeled projections (JLARC: $14–$37 a month by 2040 in Dominion territory), not measured bill changes.
Research on whether load growth raises or lowers prices is mixed: it lowered average prices through 2024, the link was not significant for residential prices, and it may not hold for future growth.
Whether new rate classes such as Virginia’s GS-5 (effective January 1, 2027) will protect other customers is not yet known.
Backup-generator health-cost estimates come from a modeled preprint; the larger figure assumes maximum permitted emissions, while JLARC finds generators run mostly for maintenance.
Data-center tax revenue is uneven: from under 1% to 31% of total local revenue in five mature Virginia localities; Loudoun County is an extreme case.
No inspected source measures the overall net effect of a data center on a whole community, and no inspected source documents a host community being destroyed.

The primary PJM market-monitor report, Virginia’s Annual Comprehensive Financial Report, New York’s executive order text and the full JLARC report were not opened; only the summaries or news reports listed in the brief were used.
review_status: AI evidence review completed; human editorial review pending
